title: Episode 272: Jonas Salk: The Polio Vaccine, the Cutter Incident, and Refusing to Patent the Sun
description:
The selfless and revolutionary life of Dr. Jonas Salk: the American medical researcher who conquered paralytic poliomyelitis, the terrifying disease that paralyzed tens of thousands of children every summer. Working in a basement laboratory at the University of Pittsburgh, Salk defied scientific orthodoxy by proving that a chemically killed virus could stimulate robust, life-saving immunity without causing disease. Tested on nearly two million schoolchildren in the massive 1954 field trials, the vaccine was declared safe, potent, and effective in April 1955. When asked by Edward R. Murrow who owned the patent, Salk replied with immortal humility: 'There is no patent. Could you patent the sun?' Discover the medical savior of a generation.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, our Top 50 Famous Non-President Americans series celebrates the physician whose scientific brilliance and selfless generosity eradicated the most dreaded childhood plague of the twentieth century. Here is George with the inspiring story of Dr. Jonas Salk.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE IMMIGRANT SON OF EAST HARLEM: 1914 TO 1939
Born in October 1914 in East Harlem, New York, Jonas Edward Salk was the eldest of three sons of Daniel and Dora Salk, Russian-Jewish immigrants who worked long hours in the garment industry and had never attended formal high school. Instilled by his parents with a fierce reverence for learning and a desire to help humanity, young Jonas attended Townsend Harris Hall, a tuition-free public high school for gifted boys, followed by the City College of New York. While his parents hoped he would become a lawyer, Jonas fell in love with laboratory biology and chemistry, entering the New York University School of Medicine in 1934. Rather than seeking a lucrative private clinical practice, Salk was drawn to medical research, later remarking that his goal was not to practice medicine on one patient at a time, but to benefit humankind in the broadest possible measure. Working under the mentorship of Dr. Thomas Francis Jr., a leading virologist, Salk helped develop the first effective killed-virus influenza vaccine for the United States Army during World War Two, mastering the delicate techniques of virus cultivation and chemical inactivation that would define his life's destiny.  His father Daniel took enormous pride in his son's intellectual promise, working twelve-hour shifts at the sewing machine to ensure young Jonas never had to abandon his studies to support the household. At City College, a tuition-free beacon for working-class immigrant children, Jonas excelled in microbiology, developing an obsessive fascination with the delicate chemical bridges that connect microscopic pathogens to the human bloodstream. Working with Thomas Francis Jr. at the University of Michigan during the war, Salk learned that chemical inactivation using formaldehyde required exquisite temperature regulation, discovering that even minor variations in ambient pH could alter the antigenic shape of viral surface spikes.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE SUMMER TERROR OF THE IRON LUNG: 1940S TO 1950S
By the late 1940s, poliomyelitis—infantile paralysis—was the most terrifying public health nightmare in the United States. Every summer, as temperatures rose, mysterious epidemics struck affluent suburban neighborhoods and crowded cities alike, paralyzing healthy children without warning. Municipalities closed public swimming pools, bowling alleys, movie theaters, and summer camps; parents kept children indoors, terrified by every summer fever or stiff neck. Hospital wards were filled with rows of iron lungs—clanking metal respirators that maintained artificial breathing for paralyzed children whose diaphragms had ceased to function. In 1952, the epidemic reached its horrifying peak: fifty-eight thousand cases were reported in the United States alone, leaving over twenty-one thousand victims with permanent paralysis and killing more than three thousand. The National Foundation for Infantile Paralysis, founded by President Franklin D. Roosevelt and financed by millions of dimes collected by ordinary citizens in movie theaters, desperately sought a cure.  The psychological terror inflicted by polio in post-war America was unprecedented: unlike tuberculosis or cholera, which predominantly afflicted impoverished urban tenements, polio struck clean, modern suburban neighborhoods with equal ferocity, turning affluent summer sunshine into a season of dread. Movie theaters distributed coin canisters bearing the portrait of Franklin D. Roosevelt, collecting millions of nickels and dimes from schoolchildren in an extraordinary nationwide philanthropic mobilization known as the March of Dimes. Families living near isolation hospitals endured the heartbreaking spectacle of watching pediatric ambulances arrive around the clock, their children whisked away into sterile wards where parents were only permitted to wave through double-paned glass windows.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE HERESY OF THE KILLED VIRUS: PITTSBURGH 1947 TO 1953
In 1947, Salk accepted a position at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine, setting up a virus research laboratory in the drafty basement of the Municipal Hospital for Contagious Diseases. At the time, medical orthodoxy, led by prominent virologists such as Albert Sabin, insisted that lasting immunity could only be produced by a live, attenuated virus that caused a mild, subclinical infection. Salk boldly rejected this view as a dangerous dogma, arguing that a live virus always carried an inherent risk of mutating back into a virulent form and paralyzing the recipient. Salk proposed that by using formaldehyde, he could chemically destroy the infective reproductive machinery of the polio virus while preserving its precise surface protein architecture. When injected into the body, the immune system would recognize these inactive antigens, producing protective neutralizing antibodies without any possibility of causing paralysis. Working sixteen-hour days with dedicated technicians, Salk cultivated the three distinct types of polio virus in monkey kidney tissue, meticulously calibrating the exact formaldehyde concentration and temperature required to kill every single virus particle.  Salk's radical departure from traditional live-virus vaccinology pitted him against Albert Sabin and John Enders, prominent virologists who publicly mocked his concept as a simplistic chemical concoction that would provide only fleeting, ephemeral protection. Undeterred by academic scorn, Salk designed a massive biological production apparatus in the basement of Pittsburgh's Municipal Hospital, using glass roller bottles to cultivate billions of virus units in cultured monkey kidney cells. Salk demonstrated that by carefully exposing the virus suspension to a one-to-four-thousand dilution of formaldehyde at zero degrees Celsius over several days, he could reduce infectivity to zero while preserving the full structural integrity of the protein shell required to train human B-cells to produce neutralizing antibodies.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE BRAVE VOLUNTEERS AND THE FAMILY TRIAL: 1953
Before conducting widespread human trials, Salk confronted profound ethical dilemmas. In 1953, he administered the experimental killed-virus vaccine to children at the D.T. Watson Home for Crippled Children and the Polk State School who were already paralyzed by one strain of polio, testing if the vaccine would elevate antibodies to the other strains without harm. The results showed a dramatic, safe surge in antibody levels. To prove his absolute confidence in the vaccine's safety, Salk sterilized hypodermic syringes on his kitchen stove and inoculated himself, his wife Donna, and their three young sons, Peter, Darrell, and Jonathan. Blood tests confirmed that the entire Salk family developed high levels of protective antibodies with zero adverse reactions. In March 1953, Salk announced his promising findings over national radio during a CBS broadcast, igniting immense hope across a terrified nation while drawing fierce criticism from skeptical medical rivals who accused him of rushing recklessly to the public press.  The preliminary trials at the Watson Home and Polk State School required agonizing moral contemplation: Salk insisted that no child should ever be subjected to greater risk than his own flesh and blood, leading to his legendary decision to inoculate his own household first. In the quiet kitchen of their Pittsburgh home, Salk boiled his glass hypodermic syringes and metal needles in a saucepan on the stove, meticulously drawing measured doses of the experimental fluid to inject into his wife Donna and their three young sons. When subsequent blood serum assays proved that every family member generated overwhelming titers of neutralizing antibodies against all three polio serotypes with zero fever or local swelling, Salk knew that the dreaded scourge was finally conquerable.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE POLIO PIONEERS AND THE APRIL 12 MIRACLE: 1954 TO 1955
In the spring of 1954, the National Foundation launched the largest public health experiment in American history, involving 1.8 million school children known as the 'Polio Pioneers'. Led by Salk's former mentor Dr. Thomas Francis Jr. of the University of Michigan, the massive double-blind trial administered the Salk vaccine, a placebo salt solution, or observed control monitoring across forty-four states. On April 12, 1955—the tenth anniversary of Franklin D. Roosevelt's death—over five hundred scientists and reporters crowded into Rackham Auditorium at Ann Arbor. Dr. Francis stepped to the podium and delivered the historic verdict: the vaccine was 'safe, potent, and effective,' showing eighty to ninety percent efficacy against paralytic polio. Church bells peeled across America, factory whistles blew, synogogues and churches held thanksgiving services, and people openly wept in the streets. Jonas Salk was instantly elevated into a global secular saint.  The 1954 nationwide field trial was an extraordinary triumph of grassroots civic organization, mobilizing over three hundred thousand doctors, nurses, public health officers, and schoolteachers who volunteered their time without a single cent of federal funding. In classrooms across America, millions of children lined up bravely to receive their shots, proudly wearing red-white-and-blue pins declaring them 'Polio Pioneers'. When Dr. Francis delivered his historic proclamation at Ann Arbor on April 12, 1955, the national relief was so overwhelming that corporate boardrooms halted meetings, stock exchanges paused trading, and department stores broadcast the radio report over public address systems while shoppers knelt in prayer.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE CUTTER TRAGEDY AND 'COULD YOU PATENT THE SUN?': 1955
Amid the nationwide euphoria, disaster struck barely two weeks later. Batches of vaccine manufactured by Cutter Laboratories in California had not been properly treated with formaldehyde, leaving live, active virus in hundreds of vials. Over two hundred children were paralyzed and eleven died, causing the federal government to temporarily suspend the entire vaccination campaign. Salk worked around the clock with federal inspectors to institute rigorous batch-testing protocols and independent safety oversight. When the program resumed with tighter standards, polio cases plummeted from tens of thousands per year to a few hundred within a decade. During a live television interview with CBS newsman Edward R. Murrow, Murrow asked who owned the patent on the vaccine. Salk gazed at Murrow with calm, unpretentious humility and replied: 'Well, the people, I would say. There is no patent. Could you patent the sun?' Had Salk patented the vaccine, economists estimated his royalties would have exceeded seven billion dollars, but Salk chose to gift his scientific breakthrough freely to the children of the world.  The catastrophic failure at Cutter Laboratories stemmed from inadequate filtration protocols that allowed microscopic clumps of active virus particles to survive formaldehyde inactivation, highlighting the perilous knife-edge between biological salvation and pharmaceutical disaster. Salk immediately joined federal inspection teams to rewrite commercial manufacturing standards, establishing mandatory tissue-culture safety tests that permanently eliminated contaminated lots from the commercial supply chain. Salk's legendary refusal to patent the vaccine was an organic expression of his personal moral philosophy, believing that life-saving scientific breakthroughs belonged to the common patrimony of human civilization rather than private corporate monopolies.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE SALK INSTITUTE AND THE CATHEDRAL OF HUMANIST SCIENCE
Despite his international adoration, Salk was denied membership in the prestigious National Academy of Sciences by envious academic peers who resented his celebrity and popular acclaim. Unbothered by academic elitism, Salk channeled his energies into creating the Salk Institute for Biological Studies in La Jolla, California. Collaborating with master architect Louis Kahn, Salk designed a stunning modernist sanctuary of poured concrete, teak, and travertine marble overlooking the Pacific Ocean, dedicated to bridging the gap between biological sciences and humanistic philosophy. In his later years, Salk worked tirelessly on researching an AIDS vaccine and published books on evolutionary philosophy, championing human wisdom and responsibility. Passing away in June 1995 at age eighty, Dr. Jonas Salk's noble legacy endures in millions of people who walk, run, and live today because one humble physician believed that science was a sacred trust for the betterment of all human life.  Salk's architectural collaboration with Louis Kahn produced one of the supreme masterpieces of twentieth-century modernism, featuring two symmetrical laboratory wings flanking a travertine plaza split by a slender, tranquil stream of water flowing toward the Pacific horizon. Salk insisted that the laboratory interiors feature completely open, column-free floor plates with accessible utility chases, ensuring that future generations of researchers could reconfigure their scientific spaces without physical barriers. In his final decades, Dr. Salk warned that humanity must evolve from competitive Darwinian survival toward conscious planetary cooperation, demonstrating through his own selfless life that scientific intellect achieves its highest glory only when harnessed to universal human compassion.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. Dr. Jonas Salk's scientific triumph and selfless refusal to profit from human suffering stand as an eternal monument to the highest ideals of medicine. Join us next week as Rebecca returns with the fearless ecological journey of Rachel Carson and the writing of Silent Spring. Until then, stay curious.
